summary: Gives short descriptive acronyms to the three numeric fields of the TLSA record used by DANE, because people kept getting confused when discussing them. It also updates the format of the IANA registry created by RFC 6698 to carry these names.

plainLanguage.summary: A box has three dials with only numbers on them, and everyone keeps mixing them up. This document sticks name labels on the dials so people can talk about them easily.

subtitle: Short names for the three numeric fields of a TLSA record, added to the IANA DANE registries.

tldr.problem: People discussing DANE kept getting confused about what the three numeric TLSA fields mean and even what order they come in.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an acronym column to the three IANA sub-registries, covering certificate usage, selector and matching type.
tldr.outcome: The DANE protocol itself does not change. The acronyms are for human use, and parsers are expected to accept them in any letter case. It updates RFC 6698.

today: RFC 7218 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6698. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Confusing Numbers
sections.content:
While discussing how to add DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE, RFC 6698) to new protocols, people were repeatedly confused about what the numeric values of a TLSA record stood for, and even the order of its fields. The RFC notes that TLSA is a name, not an acronym.

It adds an acronym column to the IANA registry definition to reduce the confusion. It does not change the DANE protocol in any way, and DANE parsers in applications and DNS software are expected to be able to parse the acronyms.
sections.plainLanguage: People kept mixing up which number meant what. Names are easier to remember than numbers.

sections.title: The Three Registries
sections.content:
IANA added an acronym column to each sub-registry of the DANE Parameters registry. Since acronyms are for human consumption, case does not matter, and software that parses TLSA records is expected to accept upper, mixed or lower case.

  • Certificate Usages: 0 is PKIX-TA, 1 is PKIX-EE, 3 is DANE-EE, and 255 is PrivCert for private use.
  • Selectors: 0 is Cert (full certificate), 1 is SPKI (SubjectPublicKeyInfo), and 255 is PrivSel.
  • Matching Types: 0 is Full (no hash), 1 is SHA2-256, 2 is SHA2-512, and 255 is PrivMatch.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the three dials now has names printed next to the numbers, like a label saying which setting is which.

sections.title: Using the Acronyms
sections.content: The RFC shows TLSA records written with acronyms in place of numbers, for example _666._tcp.first.example. TLSA PKIX-TA CERT SHA2-512 {blob}. It also shows how a specification can use them. A protocol named FOO might allow only TLSA records using PKIX-EE and DANE-EE, with selector SPKI and SHA2-512.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of saying "settings one, one, two", you can say the names, and everyone knows what you mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document only changes registry fields and does not change the behavior of any protocol. The hope is that reducing confusion leads to better specifications and operations.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the labels changed, not how the box works, so nothing gets less safe.

references.text: Hoffman, P. and J. Schlyter, "The DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol: TLSA", RFC 6698, August 2012.
